questions.stem: A 34-year-old client reports feeling anxious and shaky for 2 months and has lost 6 kg without trying. The nurse notes bulging eyes and an enlarged thyroid. Which other findings should the nurse expect?

options.text: Heat intolerance, frequent stools and a heart rate of 112/min
Cold intolerance, constipation and a resting heart rate of 54/min
Dry, coarse hair and puffy skin around the eyes
Slow speech and a delayed relaxation of the reflexes

rationale.correct: Hyperthyroidism: weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia, nervousness, diarrhea and, in Graves disease, exophthalmos.

perOption.a: Excess thyroid hormone speeds metabolism, causing heat intolerance, diarrhea and tachycardia.
perOption.b: These are signs of hypothyroidism.
perOption.c: These are signs of hypothyroidism.
perOption.d: These are signs of hypothyroidism.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with untreated Graves disease is admitted in thyroid storm after an appendectomy. The temperature is 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), the heart rate is 156/min, and the client is agitated. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Propylthiouracil (PTU) 200 mg by mouth every 4 hours
Propranolol 40 mg by mouth every 6 hours
Aspirin 650 mg every 4 hours for the fever
A cooling blanket set to 37 °C

rationale.correct: Thyroid storm: an antithyroid drug, then iodine, a beta-blocker, steroids, acetaminophen and cooling; avoid aspirin.

perOption.a: PTU blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and conversion.
perOption.b: Beta-blockers control the heart rate and adrenergic symptoms.
perOption.c: Aspirin displaces thyroid hormone from its binding proteins and can worsen the storm; acetaminophen is used instead.
perOption.d: External cooling is appropriate.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who started methimazole 6 weeks ago calls the clinic with several concerns. Which report should the nurse address first?

options.text: A fever of 38.6 °C and a sore throat since yesterday
Mild itching on both arms that starts after a hot shower
Feeling calmer and sleeping better than before
A weight gain of 1.5 kg over the past month

rationale.correct: Thionamides (methimazole, PTU) can cause agranulocytosis; clients report fever and sore throat right away.

perOption.a: These can signal agranulocytosis, a serious adverse effect; a WBC count is needed now.
perOption.b: Mild itching or rash is a minor effect.
perOption.c: This shows the drug is working.
perOption.d: This is expected as metabolism normalizes.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client received an oral dose of radioactive iodine for hyperthyroidism this morning and is going home. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll flush the toilet twice each time I use it for a few days."
"I'll use my own utensils and wash them separately."
"I'll babysit my newborn grandson this weekend as planned."
"I'll sleep alone in the spare room for a few nights."

rationale.correct: After radioactive iodine, limit close contact, especially with children and pregnant people, and follow hygiene precautions for the time specified.

perOption.a: This reduces radiation exposure from urine.
perOption.b: Saliva may contain radioactive iodine.
perOption.c: Close, prolonged contact with infants, children and pregnant people is avoided for several days.
perOption.d: This reduces exposure to others.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach precautions after radioactive iodine therapy.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old client newly prescribed levothyroxine 50 mcg also takes a calcium supplement and an iron tablet each morning. How should the nurse teach the client to take the levothyroxine?

options.text: Before breakfast on an empty stomach, apart from calcium and iron
At bedtime with a small snack so that it doesn't upset the stomach
With the calcium and iron so all three are taken together
Only on days when the client feels tired or cold

rationale.correct: Levothyroxine: take on an empty stomach, separate it from calcium and iron by 4 hours, and report palpitations or chest pain, which are signs of excess.

perOption.a: Food, calcium and iron reduce absorption, and consistent timing keeps levels steady.
perOption.b: Food reduces absorption.
perOption.c: Calcium and iron bind levothyroxine.
perOption.d: It is taken every day, usually for life.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client with untreated hypothyroidism is brought in from home in winter. The temperature is 34.2 °C (93.6 °F), respirations are 8/min, the heart rate is 48/min, and the client is barely rousable. What is the priority?

options.text: Rewarm the client quickly with a forced-air heating blanket
Support the airway and breathing
Give the client's levothyroxine by mouth with water
Start IV fluids at a fast rate for the low heart rate

rationale.correct: Myxedema coma is an emergency: support breathing, then give IV levothyroxine and corticosteroids, rewarm passively and correct sodium and glucose.

perOption.a: Rapid active rewarming can cause vasodilation and collapse, and it is not the first priority.
perOption.b: Myxedema coma causes hypoventilation and respiratory failure, so airway and breathing come first.
perOption.c: IV thyroid hormone is used, and only after the airway is secure.
perOption.d: Fluids are given cautiously because of the risk of fluid overload and hyponatremia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The clinic nurse is comparing the findings of two clients, one with untreated hyperthyroidism and one with untreated hypothyroidism. For each finding, choose the condition it is more consistent with.

rows.text: Weight gain with a smaller appetite

rationale.correct: Hyperthyroid: everything speeds up. Hypothyroid: everything slows down.

perOption.r1:c1: Thyroid hormone increases the heart rate.
perOption.r2:c1: Hyperthyroidism speeds the bowel and causes diarrhea.
perOption.r2:c2: A slowed metabolism slows the bowel.
perOption.r4:c1: Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss with a bigger appetite.
perOption.r4:c2: A slowed metabolism leads to weight gain.
perOption.r5:c2: This is not a feature of hypothyroidism.
perOption.r6:c2: Hypothyroidism causes dry skin and coarse hair.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell hyperthyroidism from hypothyroidism by findings.

questions.stem: A client is returning to the surgical unit after a total thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer. Which items should the nurse make sure are at the bedside?

options.text: Calcium gluconate and an emergency tracheostomy set
Potassium chloride and a straight urinary catheter kit
Regular insulin and a capillary glucose meter
A heparin infusion and an extra infusion pump

rationale.correct: After thyroidectomy, watch for airway obstruction, hemorrhage, hypocalcemia (tetany) and thyroid storm.

perOption.a: Hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury and airway obstruction are the main early risks.
perOption.b: These are not specific to thyroidectomy.
perOption.c: These are not specific to thyroidectomy.
perOption.d: These are not specific to thyroidectomy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the day after a parathyroidectomy, a client reports numbness and tingling of the fingers and around the mouth. When the nurse taps the client's cheek just in front of the ear, the corner of the mouth twitches. What does this suggest?

options.text: Hypocalcemia
Hypercalcemia
Hyperkalemia
Expected recovery

rationale.correct: Watch for hypocalcemia after parathyroid or thyroid surgery: tingling, and Chvostek and Trousseau signs.

perOption.a: A positive Chvostek sign indicates hypocalcemia from reduced parathyroid hormone.
perOption.b: Hypercalcemia reduces neuromuscular excitability.
perOption.c: This is not a sign of hyperkalemia.
perOption.d: Facial twitching and numbness are not expected.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old client has had fatigue, weight loss and dizziness when standing for several months. The nurse notes darkened skin on the knuckles and gums. Which laboratory findings fit the suspected diagnosis of Addison disease?

options.text: Sodium 128, potassium 5.6 and glucose 62
Sodium 146, potassium 3.1 and glucose 210
Sodium 138, potassium 4.2 and glucose 96
Sodium 150, potassium 3.4 and glucose 88

rationale.correct: Addison disease: fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia and hyperpigmentation.

perOption.a: Lack of cortisol and aldosterone causes salt wasting, potassium retention and hypoglycemia.
perOption.b: These fit Cushing syndrome or aldosteronism.
perOption.c: These are normal results.
perOption.d: A high sodium and low potassium do not fit aldosterone deficiency.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with Addison disease stopped taking hydrocortisone 3 days ago because of vomiting and now has severe weakness and abdominal pain. Highlight the findings consistent with adrenal crisis.

rationale.correct: Adrenal crisis: shock, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia, often triggered by stopping steroids or by physical stress.

perOption.r1: Severe hypotension and shock are the main danger in adrenal crisis.
perOption.r5: A normal temperature does not point to adrenal crisis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges

questions.stem: A client in adrenal crisis has a blood pressure of 78/46, a glucose of 58 mg/dL and a potassium of 5.9 mEq/L. Which set of prescriptions should the nurse give first?

options.text: IV hydrocortisone with IV 0.9% sodium chloride and dextrose
Oral fludrocortisone with salty broth and fluids by mouth
IV potassium chloride to stabilize the heart rhythm right away
IV regular insulin with dextrose for the potassium level

rationale.correct: Adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone, IV saline with dextrose, and monitoring of electrolytes and glucose.

perOption.a: Replacing cortisol and volume, with glucose, reverses the shock and hypoglycemia.
perOption.b: Oral treatment is too slow in a crisis.
perOption.c: The potassium is already high.
perOption.d: Insulin would worsen the hypoglycemia, and cortisol replacement corrects the potassium.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with Cushing syndrome from long-term prednisone has a round face, thin skin with bruises, a glucose of 186 mg/dL and a blood pressure of 152/94. Which nursing problem is the priority?

options.text: Risk for infection
Disturbed body image related to the round face
Lack of knowledge about the diagnosis
Risk for hypoglycemia between meals

rationale.correct: Cushing syndrome: moon face, buffalo hump, hyperglycemia, hypertension, hypokalemia, thin skin and infection risk.

perOption.a: Excess cortisol suppresses immunity and hides the usual signs of infection.
perOption.b: This matters, but physical risks come first.
perOption.c: This is a lower priority.
perOption.d: Cushing syndrome causes hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for 3 months. The provider plans to stop it. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll keep taking it with breakfast to protect my stomach."
"I'll stop taking it as soon as my joints feel better."
"I'll keep checking my blood sugar as I was shown."
"I'll stay away from people who are sick with colds."

rationale.correct: Long-term corticosteroids suppress the adrenal glands; they are tapered, never stopped abruptly.

perOption.a: Food reduces stomach irritation.
perOption.b: Stopping suddenly after long-term use can cause adrenal crisis; the dose is tapered.
perOption.c: Steroids raise glucose.
perOption.d: Steroids increase infection risk.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client has taken prednisone 15 mg daily for a year for polymyalgia rheumatica. Which adverse effects should the nurse monitor for? Select all that apply.

options.text: High blood glucose
Loss of bone density
Infections with few signs
Weight gain and fluid retention
Mood changes or trouble sleeping
Low blood glucose between meals
Thickened, tougher skin

rationale.correct: Steroid adverse effects: hyperglycemia, infection, osteoporosis, weight gain, mood changes, thin skin, peptic ulcers and adrenal suppression.

perOption.a: Steroids increase glucose production.
perOption.b: Steroids reduce bone formation.
perOption.c: Steroids suppress immunity and blunt fever.
perOption.d: Steroids increase appetite and retain sodium.
perOption.e: Steroids can cause euphoria, irritability, insomnia or psychosis.
perOption.g: Steroids thin the skin and make it bruise easily.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with suspected pheochromocytoma has episodes of severe headache, sweating and a racing heart. The blood pressure during an episode was 230/124. Which action should the nurse avoid?

options.text: Checking the blood pressure often, including during episodes
Palpating the abdomen deeply during the assessment
Collecting a 24-hour urine for catecholamines
Keeping the room quiet and limiting stimulation

rationale.correct: Pheochromocytoma: avoid abdominal palpation; alpha-blockade is given before surgery.

perOption.a: Frequent monitoring is needed.
perOption.b: Pressing on the tumor can release catecholamines and trigger a hypertensive crisis.
perOption.c: This is the diagnostic test.
perOption.d: This reduces triggers.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent a hypertensive crisis in pheochromocytoma.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old client has hypertension that remains above 160/100 on three medications and has a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. The client takes no diuretic, eats a normal diet and reports muscle weakness and frequent urination at night. The sodium is 145 mEq/L. Which disorder does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Primary aldosteronism
Addison disease
Hypothyroidism
Diabetes insipidus

rationale.correct: Primary aldosteronism: resistant hypertension with hypokalemia; treatment is spironolactone or surgery.

perOption.a: Excess aldosterone retains sodium and water, causing hypertension, and wastes potassium.
perOption.b: Addison disease causes hypotension and hyperkalemia.
perOption.c: Hypothyroidism does not typically cause hypokalemia.
perOption.d: DI causes hypernatremia and polyuria.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with small-cell lung cancer has a sodium of 124 mEq/L, a urine specific gravity of 1.030 and a 2 kg weight gain without edema. The blood pressure is normal, and the client takes no diuretics. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH
Central diabetes insipidus
Dehydration from poor intake
Heart failure with fluid overload

rationale.correct: SIADH: dilutional hyponatremia, concentrated urine and weight gain without edema; often caused by lung cancer, head injury or certain drugs.

perOption.a: Excess ADH retains water, diluting the sodium while the urine stays concentrated.
perOption.b: DI causes dilute urine and a high sodium.
perOption.c: Dehydration causes weight loss and a high sodium.
perOption.d: Heart failure usually causes edema.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with SIADH after a head injury has a sodium of 129 mEq/L and mild headache. Which intervention should the nurse expect to be prescribed?

options.text: Fluid restriction of 800 to 1,000 mL a day
Encouraging the client to drink 2 L of water a day
An IV infusion of 0.45% sodium chloride
Intranasal desmopressin twice a day

rationale.correct: Treat SIADH with fluid restriction and by treating the cause; hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms, with seizure precautions.

perOption.a: Restricting fluids reduces water retention.
perOption.b: Extra water worsens hyponatremia.
perOption.c: Hypotonic fluid lowers sodium further.
perOption.d: Desmopressin acts like ADH and would worsen SIADH.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is 12 hours past a transsphenoidal hypophysectomy. Urine output has been 400 mL/hr for 3 hours, with a specific gravity of 1.002. The client is very thirsty. Complete the sentence.

content.template: These findings suggest {{b1}}, and the nurse should anticipate a prescription for {{b2}}.

options.text: diabetes insipidus
SIADH
diabetic ketoacidosis
desmopressin
furosemide
fluid restriction

rationale.correct: Diabetes insipidus: polyuria, very dilute urine (specific gravity below about 1.005), thirst and a rising sodium.

perOption.b1:a: Large volumes of dilute urine after pituitary surgery suggest ADH deficiency.
perOption.b1:b: SIADH causes low urine output with concentrated urine.
perOption.b1:c: There is no evidence of hyperglycemia or ketosis.
perOption.b2:b: A diuretic would worsen the fluid loss.
perOption.b2:c: Restricting fluids would cause severe dehydration.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes insipidus who started desmopressin 4 days ago reports a headache and nausea and has gained 2 kg in 2 days. The client has kept drinking 4 L of water a day. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Water intoxication with hyponatremia
Dehydration from the diabetes insipidus
The expected effect of the medicine
High blood glucose from the desmopressin

rationale.correct: Desmopressin: monitor weight, intake and output and sodium; report headache, confusion and weight gain.

perOption.a: Too much ADH effect plus high intake retains water; headache, nausea and weight gain are early signs.
perOption.b: Weight gain suggests fluid retention, not loss.
perOption.c: A rapid 2 kg gain with symptoms is not expected.
perOption.d: Desmopressin does not affect glucose.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the second day after a transsphenoidal hypophysectomy, a client has clear, watery fluid dripping from the nose when leaning forward and reports a headache. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the client to blow the nose gently to clear the fluid
Test the drainage for glucose and notify the surgeon
Pack the nose with sterile gauze to stop the drip
Encourage coughing and deep breathing every hour

rationale.correct: After transsphenoidal surgery: avoid coughing, sneezing, blowing the nose and bending over, and report clear drainage, which may be CSF.

perOption.a: Blowing the nose raises pressure and can worsen a leak.
perOption.b: Clear drainage that is positive for glucose suggests cerebrospinal fluid.
perOption.c: Packing does not address a CSF leak.
perOption.d: Coughing raises intracranial pressure and should be avoided.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a CSF leak after pituitary surgery.

questions.stem: A client with Graves disease has exophthalmos and reports gritty, dry eyes, especially in the morning. Which intervention helps protect the client's eyes?

options.text: Artificial tears during the day and a raised head of the bed
Bright room lighting so the client can see clearly
Keeping the eyes uncovered at night so they can breathe
Limiting fluids to reduce the swelling around both of the eyes

rationale.correct: Exophthalmos care: artificial tears, sunglasses, a raised head of the bed and taping the eyelids at night if needed.

perOption.a: Lubrication protects the cornea, and elevation reduces swelling behind the eyes.
perOption.b: Bright light irritates the eyes; dark glasses help.
perOption.c: The eyelids may need to be taped closed at night to protect the cornea.
perOption.d: This does not help the eyes.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
